facts.claim: 'By My Side' is the second single from The Paper Kites' fifth studio album Roses and was released on 25 September 2020 with a video.
Roses was produced by Sam Bentley and Tom Iansek (of #1 Dads and Big Scary).
Nettwerk calls the song a restrained, delicate love song, with guest vocals from Irish singer-songwriter Rosie Carney.
Discogs credits 'By My Side' as recorded by Tom Iansek, with additional recording by Rosie Carney and Sam Bentley.

Sam Bentley recalled that Rosie Carney recorded her vocal on the floor of her London flat. She was worried because she was not used to recording without an engineer. She then sent the vocals to the band.
The band says Rosie Carney was in a hard lockdown when she recorded her part. Most of the album's music was recorded early in 2020, before Melbourne's harsher second-wave lockdown.
Sam Bentley said Roses is 'an album of duets', made of songs the band had written and wanted to record with these artists. It was about finding the right voices for each song.
Bentley said he wrote the Roses songs after listening closely to the chosen singers' records, aiming for songs he thought they could sing well.
Reviewer George Graham describes 'By My Side' as the album's closing track, a melancholy love song with a piano-based arrangement and a little steel guitar that sounds distinctive within the album.

The Paper Kites are a Melbourne indie-folk band formed in 2009 by Sam Bentley and Christina Lacy. Roses followed their 2018 album On the Corner Where You Live, which earned an ARIA nomination, and is a collection of duets.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Australian indie-folk tradition of The Paper Kites, which sources describe as lush harmonies, introspective lyrics and understated, restrained songwriting, here in a duet format.

draft:
"And if I ran then I would run to you." That line in **By My Side** does a lot of quiet work. It admits that running has crossed the narrator's mind, then bends the escape back into the promise. Even the getaway has a destination. The whole song works the same way: love declared through a pile of wants, stacked one on top of another until they start to sound like a vow.

Count how often the lyric says "I want." To take you in my arms, to talk with you, to vanish in the night with you. Then comes the little tag "I do," tacked onto the ends of lines like a reassurance, as if the singer is answering a doubt nobody voiced out loud, maybe their own. Nothing here is clever, and that's the point. Dressing it up would be a way to hide.

The best line is the most modest one: "I'm gonna make some kind of life for you / Any way I can." "Some kind" is an honest phrase. There's no plan and no picture of the house, just willingness, plus a quiet admission that the means might be thin. Pride and uncertainty share the same breath. The chorus pares things down further, "By my side" answered by fragments like "The only place," as if full sentences are more than the feeling needs.

The music matches that restraint. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar turns over a steady arpeggio while piano holds long, sustained chords underneath. The tempo is slow, the groove gentle and flowing. The lead voice is soft and breathy, close to the ear, with a slight melancholy that keeps the devotion from tipping into sweetness. Everything is clean and polished. Sam Bentley and Tom Iansek produced *Roses*, and Iansek recorded the track. Critic George Graham heard it as the album's closing track, a melancholy, piano-based love song, with a little steel guitar that sets it apart from the rest of the record.

*Roses* is, in Bentley's words, "an album of duets," and he wrote its songs after listening closely to each guest's records, aiming for material they could sing well. So this one was built for Rosie Carney, the Irish singer-songwriter. She recorded her part on the floor of her London flat during a hard lockdown, worried because she wasn't used to working without an engineer, then sent the vocals to the band. That gives the song a strange, tender backstory: a duet about wanting someone by your side, finished by people who couldn't share a room. It's the Melbourne indie-folk band's understated style turned toward distance, longing carried by two parties apart.

The song sticks because it never claims to know how love will work out, only that the wanting is real, and it makes "any way I can" sound like the most generous promise you could hear.
